summary: A 1970 note with thoughts on a proposed real-time clock at SRI. It discusses measuring delays on the network, including delays inside hosts, and the kinds of timing tests such a clock would enable, some of which would need synchronised clocks.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 32 argues that host clocks could help measure delays inside computers as well as delays between them. Some measurements need clocks at both ends, and measuring total one-way delay requires those clocks to be synchronized.

questions: why measure delays inside network hosts
subtitle: Thoughts on using host clocks to measure network message delays.

tldr.problem: Existing network measurements did not include delays inside hosts, which could form an appreciable part of a message's total delay.
tldr.mechanism: The note considers clocks in network hosts and distinguishes measurements that need synchronized clocks from those that do not.
tldr.outcome: It proposes clock characteristics for discussion and describes a UCLA clock that could support some internal measurements.

today: The unit metadata records RFC 32 as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The document is a set of thoughts on SRI's proposed real-time clock, dated 5 February 1970.

sections.title: Measure Delays Inside Hosts
sections.content:
The note says existing network measurement facilities do not include internal host delays, which may be an appreciable part of the delay for a host-to-host message. Adding a clock to one or more network hosts could support user-oriented delay measurements.

Extending tracing to include internal host delays would require a clock at both the source and destination, but those clocks would not need to be especially accurate or synchronized. Measuring absolute overall delay from one host to another would require synchronized clocks.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages can spend time being handled inside each host, not just traveling between hosts. Measuring the full delay between two hosts requires their clocks to be synchronized.

sections.title: Suggested Clock Characteristics
sections.content:
The author suggests that the SRI real-time clock have a resolution of about 1 msec, accuracy of about 1 part in 10E7, and a range of about 24 hours. The note says a crystal-controlled clock should meet these requirements at moderate cost.

It also raises the question of how the host reads the clock. A 1 msec resolution may require a hardware clock rather than a core-memory location incremented at each clock pulse, which could require complicated interface circuitry.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal gives targets for clock resolution, accuracy and range. It also points out that the computer needs a way to read the clock quickly enough.

sections.title: UCLA's Existing Clocks
sections.content:
The note says UCLA had two clocks on its Sigma 7, including one with a resolution of about 2 msec. That clock might be useful for some internal host measurements.

However, the note says it did not have the long-term accuracy needed for absolute measurements between hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: A UCLA clock could measure some delays inside a host. The note says it was not accurate enough over the long term for absolute measurements between hosts.
